Ventricular arrhythmias (refractory)

In an uncontrolled pilot, electrical storm was suppressed during treatment in seven of 11 patients, while four did not respond and two later had recurrence without maintenance. Rat studies report changes in arrhythmia inducibility.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

In an uncontrolled pilot, electrical storm was suppressed during treatment in seven of 11 patients, while four did not respond and two later had recurrence without maintenance. Rat studies report changes in arrhythmia inducibility.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact label “Ventricular arrhythmias (refractory)” is not used in the source database. A narrow mapping to “Arrhythmia, ventricular” identifies three relevant publications: one uncontrolled human rescue pilot and two separate rat experiments. The rat studies came from one research group but used post-infarction and ischemia–reperfusion models. The human study also included 20 healthy participants for physiological measurements; they were not a randomized arrhythmia-treatment control group.

Human and clinical evidence

In the pilot, stellate-ganglion phototherapy was given to 11 patients with refractory electrical storm. The authors reported suppression during treatment in seven patients; four did not respond, and two responders later had recurrence when maintenance treatment was not continued. The study had no untreated or sham-treated patient group, so it cannot estimate comparative benefit or determine how much the intervention contributed alongside ongoing care. Measurements in the 20 healthy participants concerned autonomic and catecholamine responses rather than arrhythmia treatment (Nonoguchi et al. 2021).

Animal evidence

Two rat experiments reported reduced inducibility or incidence of ventricular arrhythmias after myocardial injury. They also measured stellate-ganglion activity, microglial activation, and inflammatory markers. These findings describe possible autonomic and inflammatory pathways in acute experimental models, not evidence of reduced mortality or recurrent arrhythmia in patients (Wang et al. 2019; Wang et al. 2019).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo study was identified for this mapped indication. Tissue measurements in the rat papers are part of those animal experiments.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The clinical pilot applied low-level laser phototherapy over the stellate-ganglion region for ten minutes twice weekly over four weeks. The available summary does not establish a single wavelength or provide a complete dose profile. The rat studies used LED protocols directed to experimental neural or cardiac targets. Their routes and models differ from the clinical pilot, and no head-to-head wavelength or dose-finding study was identified.

Interpretation

The pilot documents suppression in some patients during rescue treatment, but responses were incomplete and uncontrolled. The rat studies report related changes in experimental arrhythmias. Together they identify a clinical question for comparative study, but do not show that this approach prevents recurrence or improves survival.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for control of refractory ventricular arrhythmia
Publications and records3 articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The mapped human evidence is one uncontrolled rescue pilot of 11 patients, alongside two rat experiments. Seven patients had suppression during treatment, but four did not respond and two later had recurrence without maintenance. A larger comparative study with follow-up and prespecified recurrence and safety outcomes would be needed to assess whether the approach adds benefit to usual care.
